fields.expected: I'd want to work on technical infrastructure for scientific evaluation. Over the past year I've independently studied how research gets funded and selected, reading papers and history and talking with researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative research organizations like FROs and ARPA-style programs. I started out believing grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. Conversations changed that: I now think the bigger effect is selection, because researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and may never attempt the ones that are hard to justify in advance. What interests me now is that AI is making generation cheap while judgment stays scarce. Reviewers have limited time and domain expertise is expensive, so output can grow much faster than the capacity to assess it. The part I'd want to build is the evaluation layer: methodological validation, provenance, uncertainty, evidence tracing, and clear escalation to human experts. I've done a version of this already, designing an evaluation framework for LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard at Intelehealth and using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. Outside that, I'd be happy at an early-stage team building health or decision-support systems with real users.

fields.expected: The hardest was estimating sleep without a wearable for ClarityAtlas, the iOS product I lead technically at Open Health Intelligence. The problem was that almost every credible sleep signal assumes a device on the wrist. All I had was the phone: HealthKit step counts, gait speed, movement patterns, and Core Motion data, plus phone-interaction signals. None of those directly say "asleep." They're sparse, irregularly sampled, and absent exactly when you most want data, because a phone sitting still on a nightstand looks identical to a phone whose owner left it at home. I built a passive estimation system on top of those signals and had to decide how to handle ambiguity rather than paper over it, since a confident wrong sleep window destroys user trust faster than admitting uncertainty. I also built the backend services around it in Supabase, including a "Sleep Twins" matching system using standardized behavioral features and weighted distance, which forced the sleep estimates to be comparable across users and not just internally consistent per person. We shipped it into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30+ users, which is where I learned which failure modes actually mattered versus the ones I'd been optimizing in isolation.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was nearby. We walked over to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us get a few minutes to pitch ClarityAtlas. It was slightly absurd and I was fairly sure it wouldn't work. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Johns Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute. The reason I'm proud of it isn't the meeting itself. I'd spent most of my time before that assuming that if the engineering was good enough, the right people would eventually notice. Knocking on that door was the first time I acted on the opposite idea, which is that recruiting users, finding stakeholders, and repeatedly explaining why something should exist is its own kind of work and nobody does it for you. I've since applied that to getting pilot users, institutional support, and accelerator backing. It changed how I think about what "shipping" means.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer resonates more. The work I've found most useful has always involved going to where the problem actually lives. At Intelehealth I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages, combining facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Google Maps and weather data, and healthcare-resource availability. The modeling was the easy part. The hard part was understanding what a care decision in a rural setting actually depends on, which I could only learn from the people making those decisions. Same with the anomaly-detection system I work on at Summer Atlantic Capital, where I built the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI detection service, temporal sequence models, and a learning-to-rank layer. My main concern there isn't AUC, it's that a system producing too many alerts creates a second problem instead of solving the first, so I also built an RAG-based explanation layer so analysts can actually act on outputs. That's a forward-deployed instinct: the deliverable is a decision someone can trust, not a model. I also like owning full systems rather than isolated tickets, and I've shipped end to end before, including an iOS health product into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users.
